en: Regarding the verse-text composed by the Tang Dynasty Tiantai monk Zhànrán:
the preceding text states that "verse-text consists of both reception and understanding presented separately.

In the prior prose section, the body was identified as reception and the mind as understanding, which appears to be a case of presenting them separately. As for the statement that they are "combined":
In receiving [the teaching], one integrates it with understanding; in understanding, one integrates it with receiving—hence it is called "integration.

As for the present term "separate," each of the three karmas has its own receiving and its own understanding; although they appear to be explained together, within each individual karma there is its own distinct receiving and understanding, and thus they are called "separate."

Briefly, one must first divide the text into sections so that it may be followed according to the wording; having divided it into three parts, they are: the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion.
First, regarding the general introduction: "I have heard" indicates the oral [transmission], while "rejoiced" indicates the mental [state].
The phrase "including the Buddha" (jiān fó) means including [the words] from the Buddha; this is the inclusion of the title of the person (*śarīra*).
Since it is a general title, one uses "I have heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*).
From the words "this Dharma-sound" (*idaṃ dharmasvara*) onwards is the section on receiving [the teaching].
This explains "with a heart full of great joy.

Next, the three types of action (*trikarma*) are explained. Within the first one and a half verses concerning physical realization, the first verse concerns physical realization, and the subsequent half-verse concerns physical understanding.
Next, the eleven lines beginning with "I dwell" clarify the oral understanding; herein there are two parts:
first, nine lines clarify physical distancing, and next, two lines clarify entering the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
The first section also has two parts:
the first eight lines clarify verbal acceptance, and the next line clarifies verbal understanding, thereby accepting and understanding the past verbal transgressions.
Entering into the Dharma-nature has two parts:

The first one and a half lines clarify oral reception; the subsequent half line clarifies oral understanding, because [the Buddha] received and understood what was previously obtained through his own mouth.

Following this, in the nine and a half lines beginning with "But now," there is the mental reception and understanding: the first eight lines clarify mental reception, and the subsequent one and a half lines clarify mental understanding.

In the subsequent two and a half lines, which collectively conclude the section, the first one and a half lines summarize the reception [of the teaching], while the next line concludes the explanation. "Reception" refers to externally receiving what the Buddha has spoken; "explanation" refers to internally grasping the Buddha's intended meaning.
The reason the prose section combines with the verse to form a single meaning is that they share one and the same intent.

Furthermore, the general meaning of these nine and a half lines is to provide a summary understanding of the text; while the preceding verses describe attaining a wondrous understanding, they follow the previous text by using "understanding" (*jie*) as the name for this section. Nevertheless, within this, one must further divide it into eight parts:
the first two lines summarize the realization that the past was not real.
Next, one line of verse praises the wondrous understanding attained during the first week; this corresponds to the revelation of the ultimate truth within the section on skillful means.
Three lines of verse, conversely, praise the moment when doubts and regrets arose during the initial brief exposition at the start of the Dharma-discourse week.

One line of verse praises the chapter on the various Buddhas, while various [subsequent] lines praise the disclosure of the provisional (*upāya*), and the verse on the *utpala* flower praises the parable.
5. The single line of verse beginning with "The Buddha said" [introduces] the section on past Buddhas;
6. The single line of verse beginning with "Present" [introduces] the section on present and future Buddhas;
7. The single line of verse beginning with "Just as now" [introduces] the aforementioned section on Śākyamuni.
8. From "World-Honored One" onwards, for one and a half lines, he repents and reproaches himself, verifying that the initial doubt was his own fault.

Regarding the passage in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* concerning the "thirty-two marks of golden hue... up to the eighteen unique qualities," these are all as explained in the seventh fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan*.
The present text belongs to the Perfect Teaching (yuan), as can be seen from this exposition.

Furthermore, regarding the eighty minor marks (*anuvyañjana*), according to the text of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, the Buddha’s marks are immeasurable; that only eighty are mentioned here among his physical characteristics is because worldly sentient beings serve eighty deities, and thus the Buddha possesses these [eighty] to inspire reverence.
The meaning of the current scriptural passage is simply to provide a general summary of past errors.

However, each of the eighty minor marks possesses four *siddhāntas* (purposes) to benefit others; it is not necessarily the case that they are intended solely for the sake of the eighty deities. Therefore, every single mark is none other than an ocean of excellence.
Now, hearing that the provisional has been opened and the true revealed, one realizes the former loss; the inconceivable excellence is fully detailed below in the section on Devadatta.
As for the statement, "I have [practiced] day and night," if even the sages regard the transition from dawn to dusk as "darkness and night," what is there to be described in reflecting upon this?
Therefore, in this context, one should interpret [the meaning] according to what is indicated.

There are two levels of explanation, both based on the former teachings; within the capacity of sentient beings, this doubt exists spontaneously and obscurely, and it has not yet been made explicit—this is what is being stated here.

If there is [realization] within birth and death, this is the intent of the Mahāyāna; if there is no [realization] within birth and death, this is the intent of the Hīnayāna. Having already attained the Hīnayāna, one does not know where this realization resides.
"Chang" (taste/try) means "once.

In the past, such a doubt once arose within my mind; this was a case of contrasting the Tripitaka with the Mahayana to establish an internal and external distinction. If one now attains awakening, this doubt will surely be dispelled.
Furthermore, following the section on "birth and death," it next designates both birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa as "night," while hearing the Middle Way principle is designated as "day.
This is intended to resolve the latent doubts regarding the contrast between the Separate and Perfect [teachings] and the Tripitaka and Shared [teachings].
It was only after hearing the revelation and clarification [of the Lotus Sūtra] that this doubt was finally removed, for he had heard both the Vaipulya (Fāngděng) and Prajñāpāramitā teachings.

However, the wording in the commentary (*shùwén*) is brief; one should further explain that the true principle of the Middle Way is like the sun. In the past, while at the Great [Teaching], he heard this Middle Way principle; although he had already attained realization regarding it, a latent hesitation still arose. Because he had not yet realized it as being like the sun, the sun remained hidden. Even upon hearing a brief opening of the teaching, he still harbored this doubt.

How much more so for one who formerly dwelt in the "Small" [Vehicle], yet now hears the five Buddhas extensively reveal the real and the provisional; only then are both doubts dispelled, like the rising of the sun. Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, worldly people," the meaning is as follows:

it is a metaphor for the śrāvakas who have passed through various assemblies, where they were sometimes rebuked and sometimes praised, experiencing joy or sorrow. Having come to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they have fully undergone hardships and difficulties. They are well aware of their own practice and its benefit to others, yet they merely believed these were not within their own capacity, perceiving little distinction between themselves and others. Thus, they differ from those who began with the "various flavors" (the other sūtras). Therefore, we know that starting from a humble station, one must fully experience both the civil and military arts; by traversing shallow stages, one gains deep knowledge of what things are acceptable or unacceptable. It is like the Bodhisattva of Fragrant Accumulation, who further studied the dual streams; thus, those who began with the "grass-and-creepers" (the initial teachings) have little familiarity with the manifold practices. Nevertheless, these two paths are mutually superior or inferior, and one cannot regard them as being exclusively so.
Regarding the phrase "purification by the five flavors," this refers generally to using all five flavors for purification, not exclusively *prajñā*.

As for the *Sūtra*’s statement that "the outflow-free is inconceivable" and so forth, it was previously thought that the outflow-free state merely reached the stage of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*; now, for the first time, we know it reaches the true site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

Regarding the phrase "understanding that Māra is not Māra," etc.: formerly, having heard a different version [of the scripture], one took the Buddha to be Māra; only now does one realize that one's original ignorance was a delusion and that it was actually the Buddha—hence the statement.

Regarding the passage in the *Sūtra* that says, "The Buddha, by means of various conditions," and so forth: previously, in explaining how Śākyamuni reveals the provisional to disclose the ultimate for all Buddhas, it was stated, "I have used countless expedient means, various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression," and so on; furthermore, in each of the chapters concerning the Buddhas of the three periods, it is likewise stated, "up to and including: these teachings are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle."
Regarding the phrase "concluding the composition" (*jie cheng*) within the colophon, it may further be divided into two parts:
first, the conclusion consisting of one and a half verses; second, the completion consisting of one verse.
Within the initial conclusion, there are three sections:
The first three phrases conclude the Buddha’s voice, which is the joy of speech.
The subsequent three phrases conclude the joy of mind; furthermore, by means of hearing the Buddha, this also encompasses the body.
Thus, there is joyful delight and the removal of doubt, as well as the function of the retribution experienced through what is realized and accomplished.
To explain and establish the three preceding points: seeing the Buddha brings joy to the body; hearing the Dharma brings joy to the mouth; and awakening to understanding brings joy to the mind.
Since he was already taught the Great [Vehicle] in the past, why speak only of having the opportunity to draw near to the Buddha's person today?

Although you were temporarily deluded, what you previously heard was not erroneous; this clarifies the conditions for your hearing it again today. Even though the teaching midway through was provisional, it did not constitute a mere "Small Vehicle" teaching; that you have now recovered the hearing of it proves that your faith stems from past instruction. Verifying your current understanding against the past, it is clear that it is not in vain. Furthermore, regarding the vision of the Buddha and so forth, there are three types of penetration, each with its own threefold reception.

Regarding the phrase "the condition of seeing the Buddha": it is because of the great vision of the past that one obtains the condition for realizing the truth today; for it is only when one realizes the truth that it can truly be called "seeing.
Regarding the phrase "the condition of hearing the Dharma through remorse": from the time of the intermediate state until now, one has been led toward the Lesser Vehicle by means of grasping.
Furthermore, I have heard that the two types of ghee were explained in brief: generally, all who experience regret do so because their past [merit] was small.
As for the statement "not in vain," it means that although one originally heard of the Great [Vehicle], it is not in vain now.

Next, the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* is cited to explain "unsurpassed," and the *Ratnakūṭa-alaṃkāra Sūtra* is cited to explain the "path"; this is done by borrowing specific names to manifest the meaning of the Perfect [Teaching].
The meaning is complete while the names differ; this applies to all cases, yet others lack this intention, so it must not be applied indiscriminately.
Regarding these seven "unexcelled" (anuttara) factors, two sets are listed in the text.

In the first set, the former one is the fruit and the latter six reside in the cause. Among these six causes: the first two are harmony; the next two are merit and wisdom; and the final two are realization and practice. Although they are divided into groups of three and two, they mutually provide support for one another. Therefore, all six causes are collectively termed "unexcelled. Because one practices the causes in view of the fruit, the fruit is mentioned first and the causes follow.

Regarding the "six harmonies" (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*): first, one receives and upholds the unsurpassed [vows] through body, speech, and mind; because these three harmonies exist, one benefits oneself and others. The six harmonies of the Mahāyāna encompass all phenomena exhaustively. The two obstacles (*dvaya-āvaraṇa*) are simply the afflictive (*kleśa*) and cognitive (*jñeya*) obstacles.

Regarding these two hindrances, if discussed separately, they exist prior to their respective stages; in this case, "ignorance" refers exclusively to the "dust-like" ignorance of the external realms. If, however, one considers them comprehensively across both higher and lower stages, "ignorance" then encompasses both internal and external ignorance as well as nescience (*avidyā*). Thus, it should be understood that they differ only in terms of being expanded or condensed.

Regarding the statement that "in the supreme practice, only the noble and the Brahma [levels] without remainder are mentioned": Heaven is that which is realized; it is the fruit and function of the "sick child. By cultivating two, one realizes one, and thus possesses these two capacities. For this reason, only these two are mentioned, and the other three are not listed.

Next, regarding the "reiteration," this is established further from the perspective of the fruit; that is, the six causes are designated by names established from the fruit. By investigating these names and explaining them in detail, the intent of the sutra is revealed.

Since it concludes below by stating, "In this way, various aspects clarify the unsurpassed path," the meaning of the path is immeasurable and is established according to whichever teaching is employed; therefore, it is said here that this sutra perfectly elucidates the unsurpassed path.

This is precisely the path of the Unsurpassed Family, which is called the Unsurpassed Path; each and every unsurpassed aspect possesses the supremacy of all paths. Regarding the phrase "Although there was great transformation in the past," and so forth:

because ignorance within the realm has never been destroyed, it is called the darkness of delusion. Even if one begins with the initial mind of perfect cultivation and has not yet destroyed the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), a single phrase heard is taken as a seed within consciousness and will never be lost for eternal kalpas. When comparing darkness to light, even the darkness is not mistaken about the truth; how much more so, then, could true awakening be in vain?
Moreover, for those who have realized the Truth, there are both gradual and sudden modes of progress, as fully explained previously.

Therefore, regarding those still deluded and obscured, the "six sense organs" refers to the stage prior to them; although they have not yet shattered ignorance, because they are in the semblance-stage of non-retrogression, they are termed "not obscured."
"If one attains great understanding" and below constitutes the inquiry;
"the prediction has four meanings" and below constitutes the answer regarding the necessity for the meaning of the prediction.

These four types of prediction are fully present in all three cycles [of the Lotus Sutra]. In the middle cycle, among the four [meanings], only the character "zhōng" (middle) is excluded from within the second meaning; therefore, by the time of the final cycle, there are only three and not four.
Furthermore, among these four, the first intention encompasses the latter three.
Moreover, the first four refer to the past, while the second and third pertain only to the present.
Additionally, the first four concern only oneself, whereas the second and third relate to others.

Furthermore, regarding the third supernormal power (*abhijñā*), it will manifest as follows: the first exists only in the present; the second exists only in the future; and the fourth exists only in the past.
Jiaxiang’s ten points are verbose and lack coherence; I shall now briefly indicate them to show their complexity and conciseness:
first, to verify that the realization is not in vain.
Second, it causes the removal of doubt and regret;
these two belong to the section on "Explanatory Establishment" (*anuvyākhyāna*), so why mention "prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*) again?
Third, it induces faith in sentient beings; this belongs to the current third [section].

The fourth point causes Śāriputra to aspire toward the fruit; this belongs to the initial section of the chapter which praises the two wisdoms of the five Buddhas, intended to reveal the provisional and simultaneously cause him to aspire toward the ultimate. Now, in this instance, he is merely granted the prediction of the eight phases of enlightenment; since these are attained spontaneously at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), there is no need to speak of aspiration.

The fifth reason is for the purpose of attracting the eight classes [of supernatural beings]. To properly attract those of the same kind is primary; the attraction of the eight classes is secondary, which corresponds to the second "secondary" meaning in the present text. Previously, the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) were not recorded; therefore, their spiritual capacities were forever excluded from this hope. Now, however, they are recorded because they are included as secondary attractions among the eight classes; thus it is said that they must be recorded.
Sixth, regarding the drawing forth of beings toward rebirth, this is identical to the present intention.
Seventh, regarding the revelation of the sutra’s secrets: "secrets" pertain to principle (*li*), while the "records of the small" pertain to phenomena (*shi*).
Furthermore, what is recorded as being manifest is not termed secret; this belongs to the teachings of the past.
Eighth, "desiring to achieve the Mahāyāna" pertains to the first intention.

Ninth, "harmonizing the Great and Small Vehicles," as in the ancient account of the Buddha’s reprimand of Maitreya regarding his recognition [of his own attainment], refers to "harmonization" (he-hui) as a specific name for the "opening of the provisional" (kai-quan). It is precisely because the provisional is opened that one can then be granted a prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa).
The tenth [point], "as a condition for inducing existence" (*bhavābhinirvṛtti-pratyaya*), is also the third intention.
Although the ten intentions are numerous, their meanings are few, and they still lack the fourth intention found in the present text.

Since the original generation of the Great Mind (*mahācitta*) always anticipates the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), one knows that these ten meanings are prolix and insufficient; there are many such examples throughout the various passages of that commentary, and the rest cannot be recounted here.

Within the section on the formal bestowal of prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*), there are two textual passages each for the ten items beginning with the "causes of practice" (*pratipatti-hetu*); within the "time period" (*kāla*) there are both the world-age and the numerical count;
within the "causes of practice" there are the making of offerings to the Buddhas and the cultivation of practice;
and within the "attainment of the fruit" (*phala-prāpti*) there are both general titles and specific titles.
Within the purity of the land, there is a land named "Pure Land";

within the preaching of the Dharma, there are the three vehicles and the one vehicle. Although the scriptural text does not explicitly mention the term "one vehicle," since the vows were fulfilled by teaching both the three and the one as the correct path, the primary and the secondary are both present.
Within the names of the eons, there are both indications and explanations.
Among the various categories of numbers, there are persons and practices;
within the measure of lifespans, there is the lifespan of a Buddha and the lifespan of a human; since this discusses only the lifespan after attaining Buddhahood, the prince is excluded;
among those in the state of being the successor (the *upapadya-parivartin*), there are both the provisional and the actual.
The Dharma-abiding consists of both the real and the semblance.
Within the context of perfect purity, the name is first established; the phrase "that land" and what follows describe its characteristics.
That which is without high or low is called level (*sama*); that which is not partial is called correct (*samyak*).
"Peaceful and secure" refers to the usage regarding the lower lands; "lapis lazuli" further clarifies the superior characteristics.

Within the discourse on the Dharma, the phrase "likewise by" is used because it conforms to the present Śākyamuni. Regarding "śarīra," the following clarifies the threefold intent of the teaching: the purity of the land is singular, yet to fulfill his vows he teaches three [bodies], which are simultaneously established and simultaneously relinquished.
Question:
Where is this vow expounded?
Answer:

According to the *Mahākaruṇā-garbha-sūtra*, he practiced the bodhisattva path for sixty kalpas; when a brahmin begged for his eyes and he was about to retreat, he made a vow that on the day he attained Buddhahood, he would open the gates of the Three Vehicles of the Dharma.
Question:
Since they have already received their prediction (vyākaraṇa), why must they still pass through several more kalpas?
Answer:

If the prediction for a bodhisattva is given in general terms, such as "attaining non-arising" and so forth, the prediction for a śrāvaka must be specified in terms of kalpas and lands. Since the place where a response-buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) attains enlightenment requires specific karmic conditions, and these śrāvakas previously lacked practice directed toward a pure land, they must establish karmic connections with sentient beings after receiving their prediction; because the capacities of those beings differ, the duration of the kalpas varies.
Although the dragon girl was a female, because her vehicle was swift and she had previously practiced skillful means, this is discussed separately based on her provisional manifestation.

Furthermore, regarding the fact that the various śrāvakas appear at different times, this is for the purpose of accommodating the suitability of beings according to the length of their respective capacities; since their karmic conditions are not equal, how could their initial stages of dwelling differ?

When people of the world see the śrāvakas receive their predictions of enlightenment, they resent the vastness of the kalpas; yet when they see the dragon girl attain Buddhahood, they doubt that such a short period of time could suffice. Some suspect that for minor transgressions, the retribution is too extensive; others ponder how small virtues can bring about such abundant merit. Some deride the Buddha’s teachings on the turning away from [the mundane] as being inconsistent or indeterminate; some criticize the bodhisattvas for displaying such disparate traces of manifestation. Hearing of the superior practices spanning many kalpas, they suspect the teaching is a fabrication; hearing of the miraculous transformations of the Buddhas, they claim these are merely combined with worldly arts. Some suspect that sixty minor kalpas were but half a day; others are confused that a single kṣaṇa could last for immeasurable kalpas. Such heterodox remarks are beyond counting.
This arises because the seeds of false views are strong while the power of past cultivation is weak; thus, they sit with folded hands guarding their worn-out sophistry and debating right and wrong.
Yet, if one simply trusts the teachings and reveres the principles, why resort to arbitrary conjecture?

To respond to conditions and benefit sentient beings is not something known to the world; one should know that how could such a person understand that those in the first stage (prathamabhūmi) receive the prediction of the eight marks, manifesting as Buddhas in the ten directions through various displays? Although these various displays differ from the prediction of the Dharma-body, if one does not cultivate practices for the Pure Land for the sake of sentient beings, for whom would the land be taken when one attains Buddhahood?
Regarding the mention of "the ten powers" (*daśabala*) and so forth in the verse from the Sūtra: it is only at the stage of Buddhahood that these are designated as "powers.
At the initial stage of abiding (*prathama-vihāra*), they are designated as "merits" (*guṇa*).

As for the term "and so forth" (*ādi*): it does not refer solely to making offerings to the Buddha, but also includes practices for purifying the Buddha-land; alternatively, it may indicate that one attains the marks of prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) for the first abiding by virtue of acquiring a portion of the merits of the ten powers.

If one cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* regarding the ten types of power-constituents possessed by a bodhisattva, this clarifies that a bodhisattva who has entered the stages (*bhūmi*) is endowed with the causes for the ten powers.

As for the passage in the *Sūtra* stating, “Each removed their robes,” and so forth, this refers generally to the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings, specifically the two groups of renunciants.
What is called the "upper robe" (ūrdhvaka-cīvara) is the great robe (saṃghāṭī).

Regarding the three robes, none may be discarded; for in the Western regions, most practitioners possess only these three robes. As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, after three hundred bhikṣus heard the Prajñāpāramitā, they all used their saṃghāṭīs as offerings.
In the *Treatise*, it is sometimes said:
"The absence of marks constitutes the Dharma," and sometimes said:
"One attains it anew on that very day."

If one explains this comprehensively to include both the conventional and the ultimate—as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*—the Sūtra’s statement that “he himself turns back” indicates that upon hearing Śāriputra receive his prediction, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) spontaneously turns; thus, cause and effect, the environment and its inhabitants, and self and other all undergo transformation.
Regarding the statement in the *Sūtra* that "it is the greatest wheel of Dharma": "greatest" (*mòu*, 最) refers to the opening of the Perfect [Teaching] within the present scripture;
"great" (*dà*, 大) refers to the fourfold wondrousness of persons and so forth, or the tenfold [wondrousness] of objects and so forth, or the threefold [wondrousness] of the Buddha and so forth.
The wheel of the wondrous Dharma is called the "wondrous Dharma-wheel" (*dharmacakra*).
This is a brief correspondence between the beginning and the end; it does not describe the intermediate Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā periods, as is fully detailed in the *Xuán* (Xuanzang’s) text.
The ten matters of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra are called the "Turning of the Wheel of Dharma," which is a universal principle.
Furthermore, it is said:
the perfect sound does not correspond to the categories of great or small; it is sentient beings themselves who differ.
This would instead disparage the sublime Dharma; how then could it be called praise? How could it be termed the propagation of the sutra?

Regarding the subsequent four lines and a half that constitute the self-narration, only three names are listed. Within these, one should distinguish them as follows: the first line constitutes the self-narration; the next two lines and a half constitute sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*); and the final one line constitutes the dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*). One must explain their respective meanings by carefully correlating them with the text.

Regarding the absence of three of the five repentances: since one has already received a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), there is no sin to repent; since one has already obtained a partial prediction, there is no need for exhortation (*adhyeṣaṇā*); and since one has already reached the destination, the making of vows (*praṇidhāna*) is omitted.
However, if one looks toward the ultimate fruit, with the exception of repentance, the other four are not absent.
The five repentances are fully explained as recorded in the seventh fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan*.

Regarding the phrase "such as Śāriputra" and so forth: although only three sections are recounted among the preceding four texts, this is because the Dharma was previously heard together and need not be repeated; it merely shows that Śāriputra attained realization and so on through these three stages, implying that I too, having heard it together with him, should likewise attain it.

All these were expedient means; it was solely because the practice of the ultimate truth had not yet matured that expedient practices arose concurrently. Therefore, for over forty years, the reality was not revealed. As soon as they heard the wondrous principle of the five Buddhas, their minds were suddenly enlightened; they immediately shattered ignorance and became fit to receive the prediction of enlightenment. Once the illness of the ultimate truth was cured, the illness of expedient means also healed. How could the transformative merit of this single lifetime have been accomplished entirely through the practice of the ultimate truth alone?
Regarding the phrase "not yet healed" followed by "and so forth," one should provide a detailed account of how [the Buddhas] manifested illness and recovery in various lands.
Regarding the phrase "attaining the prediction" followed by "and so forth," this too should be set forth here; furthermore, the four subsequent sections all rely upon analogies and causal conditions.

Regarding the phrase "The subsequent passage is found in the 'Dharma Master' Chapter, etc.," this refers to the section following the account of past lives where the fourfold assembly rejoices. It points to the first part of the prose section in the "Dharma Master" Chapter; specifically, after enumerating the various classes of people belonging to the fourfold assembly and the three vehicles, it states: "All such persons as these, having heard even a single line or a single verse of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* before the Buddha, rejoice with a single thought of sympathetic joy. This is also the passage concerning their rejoicing.

Regarding the passage beginning with "Now, he newly exerts great compassion," etc.: while in the first cycle [of practice] it was primarily for the sake of resolving one's own doubts, here it is exclusively for the benefit of others as he newly exerts great compassion. This requires further cultivation of Pure Land practices, which constitute the foundation of the bodhisattva path.
Based on this interpretation, the meaning of the preceding passage can be understood.
Regarding the section beginning with "There are some people," the ancient masters’ intention was as follows:

At the start of each of the two cycles—both the Dharma and the Parable—the Venerable Śāriputra had a distinct doubt; hence they are termed "new" and "old. Since the twelve hundred disciples had not yet harbored doubts at the start of the first cycle, there was only the "new" [doubt].

Regarding the phrase "Now it is said," and so forth: those of superior capacity, upon first hearing the brief exposition, were moved from their attachments and gave rise to doubt; yet, by receiving the chapter on the Five Buddhas, they immediately attained great enlightenment.

Those of middling capacity have heavy attachments; when the brief exposition was given, their doubts were the same as those of the superior type. Since they did not awaken during the Dharma-exposition and their doubts still persist, is it not the case that those of middling capacity harbor more doubt than those of superior capacity?

Therefore, when Śāriputra himself recounted his state, saying, "I now have no further doubt or regret," he was merely describing how those twelve hundred others among his peers still possessed delusions; why then do you claim that Śāriputra himself had many doubts?
Question:

Even ordinary beings may attain awakening upon hearing just once; they have already heard the brief and extensive accounts of the five Buddhas opening the provisional, as well as the account of Śāriputra receiving his prediction after summarizing these points. Since even dragons and ghosts can cite such precedents, why do those of middling and inferior capacities remain suddenly deluded?
Answer:
There are two meanings here:
first, long-term adherence; second, entering a stage.
Understanding is the breaking of attachments; once attachments are broken, one enters and abides [in the truth]. Ordinary people lack this capacity, so they may find it difficult to comprehend.

As for Śrāvakas, although they have heard the teaching, they have not yet realized it due to two reasons: first, because their habitual attachments have persisted for a long time; second, because their root-natures differ. For these reasons, they are divided into three grades.

Regarding the *Sūtra* passage beginning with “hearing what has never been heard before,” [the commentary] states: Having heard these four sections from Śāriputra—which were absent from the former teachings—and based on the five chapters concerning the Buddhas’ teaching that “I am not the Buddha’s knowledge and vision,” he verified that what he had previously attained lacked true reality. Since he could not distinguish whether the reality of the present was the same as or different from that of the past, he is said to have harbored doubts.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the fourfold assembly, he universally entreats [the Buddha]," etc., it is asked:

In the previous discourse on the Dharma, there were likewise three [sections] before and one after; since they did not awaken upon hearing it then, why is this current entreaty for the same three before and one after any different from the former?
Answer:
What is called "causes and conditions" (nidāna) refers to the root causes and origins from the first three chapters through the final one; thus, it is termed "causes and conditions.

The chapter on the four Buddhas is brief, while that on Śākyamuni is somewhat more extensive. Although the five turbidities are used therein to explain the provisional [teachings], the beginning and end are not yet clarified; consequently, those of medium capacity do not understand this point.

This parable exhaustively elucidates the characteristics of saṃsāra, details the reasons for providing the three carts to leave the house, and simultaneously demonstrates the intent behind requesting three and then giving one; it extensively narrates the equal bestowal upon all sons and the impartiality of the father’s mind—this is precisely how the request regarding causes and conditions is fulfilled.

Among these, regarding the fourfold assembly within the aforementioned four [types of assemblies], they are not limited to the two groups of those who are "appropriately matched" (*dengji*) and those who have "established a karmic connection" (*jueyuan*); those who speak and attain understanding are precisely the two groups of those who "initiate" (*faji*) and those who are "influential echoes" (*yingxiang*).
"Resentment" (*zhuì*) means harboring grudge and hatred.

Regarding the "explanation by way of analogy," according to the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, this may be called a "universal analogy" (*biànyù*), as it applies universally to both the internal and external realms, as well as to the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles;
alternatively, it may be called a "non-analogy," for such a burning house does not exist in the mundane world.
Regarding the "beginning and end" and the "one who extinguishes the fire," it must necessarily be conveyed by means of the vehicle; first giving and later taking, first three and later one.

However, as for the metaphors and their applications (*upanaya*), they vary between being broad or concise. If the metaphor is concise while the application is broad, one first brings the text of the application to correspond with the conclusion of the metaphor; then, upon reaching the application itself, it must be explained in full detail.

If the analogy is broad while the application is brief, how could the World-Honored One have uttered such idle words? It is necessary to explain the analogy in detail, while the application need only be briefly matched.
Within the general analogy, the term "one gate" refers to what was mentioned above: that although there are various correspondences, they do not constitute various [gates], but are indeed one gate.

The previous discussion cited the "bestowal" (dāna) in relation to the Buddha-way; the Buddha-way is itself the "one gate," while the various [provisional means] constitute the exercise of skillful means (upāya).

Now, in presenting what is revealed, it speaks only of the "one gate. This is likewise each expressing its respective capacity; for when the capacity is contrasted with the object, their underlying meaning does not differ—this can be seen through reflection.

Regarding the phrase "names are like guests" and so forth: practice resides within oneself, while names are transmitted from others; thus, actual practice is intimate, whereas provisional practice is distant. When practice is intimate, the name is remote and extends throughout the three lands; when practice is distant, the name is near and exists only in the Land of Common Dwelling (*sahā-loka*). Provisional means and the land of true retribution alternate as remote and near; although intimacy and distance mutually manifest one another, the name and the practice correspond to each other without error in their transmission from others. Therefore, when practice is lofty, the name is remote, and if the name is substantial, the practice must be intimate; hence, by using the dwelling place to represent it, one verifies that the name and practice do not overlap.
Regarding the term "fengjiang" (feudal borders): "feng" refers to the limited domain under one's administration, while "jiang" refers to the divine boundary of the territory thus conferred.
A small unit is called a "bang" (state), and a large one is called a "guo" (country).
It is further said:
"When a Son of Heaven establishes a state, he takes the most distant place as his capital.
The ruler acts as the sovereign; the territory governed by the sovereign is called a 'city' (yì). Within the city, the various residential areas are termed 'villages' (jùluò)."
Therefore, the cities and villages and so forth become progressively narrower.

As for the phrase "not using the old interpretation," this refers to using only space to represent the three-thousandfold world system of the Shared Land (*sādhāraṇa-bhūmi*), while omitting the two lands of Expediency (*upāya*) and True Reward (*vipāka*); for this reason, it is not accepted.

Next, regarding the citation of the *Śāstra*’s intent: in general discussions of similarities and differences, whenever it is said that the selection and rejection of analogies differ, the *Śāstra* treats cause and effect together.
For now, let us speak briefly of the fruit and its retribution, using the analogy of a householder who has realized Buddhahood.

The meaning of cultivating the causes is not the subject of our current discussion; rather, within the context of the ultimate fruit, we shall clarify the primary reality by means of its supporting environment. While the essence of these lands is both horizontal and vertical—interpenetrating yet non-dual—we shall here discuss them solely from the perspective of their vertical function. Thus, through the disparity of their breadth and narrowness, we manifest the universal pervasiveness of the abodes.

Regarding the phrase "From the fundamental, he manifests the traces," etc.: prior to this day, from the fundamental realm of *sukhāvatī* (Jikō), he had manifested traces in the three lands; now, at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he gathers these traces of the three lands back into the fundamental realm of *sukhāvatī*.
That which accords with principle in practice is the essence;
that which is reached by name is the trace.

Since principle pervades the three lands, the scope of transformation must necessarily be universal; thus, it never happens that practice is inferior while the name is extensive. This is because the substance and its function correspond to one another; therefore, it is said there is no distinction between guest and host, meaning that name, practice, person, and land are all mutually correspondent.

If one follows the previous interpretation and does not accept the two lands, but instead takes the locus where compassion is manifested as the "country," then the distinction between the Land of Common Dwelling and the city would be lost; consequently, one would fail to understand that the country is defined by the breadth or narrowness of that compassion, thereby completely losing sight of both the land of true retribution and the land of skillful means.
"Biao" refers to the tiger's markings; "bing" means brilliance. Thus, it is a majestic appearance where the patterns are distinct and formidable.
"Yangyi" (overflowing) means being full within and abundant without.
Because it fills the interior, it is called "circulation" (*xing*);
because it suffuses the exterior, it is called "pervasion" (*bu*). As for the "Three Sovereigns" (*sanhuang*), they are Fuxi, Shennong, and Huangdi.
As for the "Five Emperors" (*wudi*), they are Shaohao, Zhuanxu, Gaosin, Tang, and Yu.
Those [Kṣatriyas] consist only of two types, such as the Kṣatriya and so forth; for now, we borrow this to categorize them by analogy.

"Huang" (Yellow) signifies the center, while "Di" (Emperor) represents a virtue that mirrors Heaven and Earth. Among the various surnames in this land, who does not inherit from him? Generally speaking, those who are not of his lineage—being biased, eccentric, or having obtained their status through separate means—are considered his original descendants.
"Yi" (裔) refers to the hem of a garment, as there is a root from which it may be inherited.
Some say that regarding "descendants" (miao-yi): "miao" (苗) refers to the initial growth of grass, which is the beginning of acquiring a clan name.
"Succession is unadulterated, like the beginning and end of a sprout.
Regarding "a sable on the left and an ornament inserted on the right," as for "sable" (*diāo*), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states:
"It resembles a mouse."
Xu Guang’s *Commentary on Vehicles and Attire* states:

"This is the crown of the Shizhong (Attendant-in-Ordinary); it has a marten fur (*diao*) on the left and a cicada (*chán*) on the right, resembling the cicada’s purity and loftiness in drinking dew and not eating."
It is further stated:
"That which is inserted on the right is the hairpin (zhan).
'The Left Aider and the Right Assistant' refers to the Chancellor."
The phrase "Yanmei A-heng" refers to the Chancellor (Xiang-wei).
This is like the case of Emperor Gaozong of Yin appointing Yue Shuo, as detailed in the seventh record of the *Zhi Guan*.
"Ā" means to lean upon; it signifies to rely or depend on.
"Héng" means level or even. Regarding "Tónglíng" and the others:
for example, there was Dèng Tōng. Emperor Wén of the Hàn dynasty dreamed that he was falling into a well and was rescued by Tōng; consequently, the Emperor summoned Tōng to his presence.
The diviners said:
"He will not escape starving to death.
The Emperor then ordered people to cast coins at the Copper Mountain in Shu to provide for him; how could he have starved to death?
Later, when Emperor Ai ascended the throne, he was accused of privately minting coins and consequently died of starvation in prison.
Some say that he had already been resented by others during the time of Emperor Wen, and thus eventually starved to death.
For the time being, let us take the example of initial wealth as stated in the *Book of Jin*:
"Shi Chong possessed the Jingu Valley, located to the east of Luoyang.
The character "yan" (延) means to advance, and it also implies to lead or guide.
This means that majesty awes others without the need for severity, being as stern and pure as frost.
"Lóng" (隆) signifies height;
being both high and weighty, one's commands are obeyed without being issued.
As for wisdom, one sits within the curtains and plans, repelling threats from ten thousand *li* away; it is like an armory—what implement would not be there?
When employed, it is put into action; when set aside, it is stored away.
"White Jasper" (Bai gui) refers to fine jade with a tapered top.
The *Shuowen Jiezi* states:
"An auspicious jade."
"Round above and square below.
The *Baihutong* states:
"Jade is that which is pure."
"Shi" (式) means to gaze up with reverence.
"One person" refers to the Son of Heaven, as the *Classic of Filial Piety* states:
"The Son of Heaven."
The World-transcending Elder is fully endowed with ten attributes:

"Buddha" refers to his lineage; "Accomplished Merit" refers to his station; "Dharma-wealth" refers to his riches; "Ten Powers" refers to his majesty; "Single-mindedness" refers to his wisdom; "Early Accomplishment" refers to his venerability; "Three Karmas" refers to his conduct; "Endowed with Buddhahood" refers to his propriety; "Ten Directions" refers to his reverence; and "Sevenfold" refers to his refuge.

If one considers the fruit in relation to the cause, it should be said that according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), from Equal Enlightenment (Dengjue) downward, because the real cause and the ultimate aspiration for enlightenment are not two different things, these ten virtues all derive from the ultimate fruit.

If, however, we proceed from the perspective of their respective divisions—the provisional and the real within the fruit—then while the names of the ten virtues remain the same across the three provisional and one real teachings, the substance underlying those names must be distinguished according to each specific teaching. Consequently, the three truths of the limit of reality (ji-zhi) differ, and even the extent of what is ultimately attained varies; therefore, although the name "Elder" is common to all, it must now be understood according to its specific distinctions. To apply a specific term to a general one would be to overstep the boundaries of the teachings.

Regarding the ten aspects of "Contemplating the Mind": "Contemplating the Mind" corresponds to one's lineage; "the three delusions" corresponds to one's station; "the three truths" corresponds to one's wealth; "correct contemplation" corresponds to one's majesty; "the Middle Way" corresponds to one's wisdom; "long-accumulated" corresponds to one's venerable age; "this contemplation" corresponds to one's conduct; "traversing conditions" corresponds to one's propriety; "being able to act thus" corresponds to one's reverence; and "devas and dragons" corresponds to one's refuge.

These ten virtues do not transcend the three categories of object, wisdom, and practice. Although one has not yet entered the [bodhisattva] stages, one is like a prince in the womb; therefore, they are called the "Ten Virtues of the Tathāgata in Contemplative Practice.

When contrasted with the supramundane, they still follow their respective teachings, distinguishing between different fruits and different contemplations. According to the teachings, the causes and effects of contemplation are distinct; thus, the three contemplations are applied to the four teachings. By fully surveying these virtuous characteristics to praise contemplation, one ensures that future learners are complete in their cultivation of the cause. By means of the ten virtues of contemplation, one achieves the ten virtues of the fruit. Because one can single-mindedly and simultaneously illuminate the three dharmas, this constitutes the full completion of the ten virtues of contemplating the mind. Therefore, passages such as "O Son of the Buddha" are cited as proof for contemplating the mind, just as the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) fully establishes the majestic deportment and so forth.

Furthermore, these ten virtues constitute the Ten Dharmas that Form the Vehicle; their sequential integration possesses profound significance. Why is this so? Because the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the correct object;

because one gives rise to vows based on principle, it is called "abiding in patience" (*kṣānti*); because the mind rests in principle, it is said to "contain" that principle; by eliminating delusions regarding the three truths, one attains the name "pervasive penetration"; because the Middle Way illuminates both poles simultaneously without obstruction or stagnation, the factors of the path of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-mārga*) transcend the seven stages of expedient means; they assist the three karmas so that they do not err against principle; because one relies on the true stage, there is no failure when facing objects; because faith and understanding are already deep, one is able to practice patient endurance; and by not giving rise to attachment to dharmas, one is able to receive offerings from below.
The three teachings and ten methods are unfolded and explained in succession to form the ten methods for contemplating the mind (*guanxin*) in this present sutra.

These ten contemplations do not merely exist horizontally within the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxingwei*); rather, from the initial stage to the end, all ten contemplations are fully present. Therefore, the meaning of these ten virtues is also profoundly vertical. Furthermore, they merge with the horizontal and vertical ten vehicles (*shicheng*), and moreover, the ten virtues correspond precisely to the meanings of the sutra text.

Regarding the phrase "comprehensive and all-encompassing through strategic allocation": because he devises plans and strategies for various parts, he possesses a comprehensive, magnanimous, and far-reaching vision.
As for the character *zī* (貲), the *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Zi means wealth."

The reason three types of "Elders" (zhǎngzhě) must be established is that the title "Elder" originally employs worldly conventions as a metaphor for the supramundane. Since there is no path to the supramundane that does not require contemplation, we know that speaking directly of the supramundane involves contemplating the mind; it does not differentiate between provisional teachings and their remote origins, yet it still maintains a balance of brevity and detail. Within this, the threefold interpretation—consisting of causes and conditions, the teaching, and the contemplation of the mind—is already established.

Regarding the phrase "Briefly, eighteen," and so forth: this explains the wisdom that serves as the basis for entry. Although the gates may be brief or extensive, they do not transcend the dwelling into which one enters.
As for what is meant by "brief and extensive": within a single object there is a single emptiness, yet each and every object can also possess all eighteen; therefore, it is said to be immeasurable.

Just as a single form or a single mind each possesses all eighteen [elements], so too does form, in relation to the sense faculties—whether the faculty is internal, the form is external, or both are together—and because this emptiness is also empty, it is called "emptiness of emptiness" (śūnyatā-śūnyatā).
If one grasps this principle, it can be understood by applying it analogously even to the case of "non-dharmas" and "dharmas.
However, speaking in general terms, because there are eighteen names for emptiness, they are called the "eighteen kinds of emptiness"; thus, it is said to be a brief exposition.

Regarding the detailed and abbreviated enumerations within these eighteen [dhātus], they are fully explained as presented in the fifth fascicle of the *Zhiguan* (Mohe Zhiguan), as well as in the *Fajie Cidi* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Regarding the phrase "If one discusses," the text below cites merit and wisdom to explain "fields and houses.

As for the expression "possessing many fields and houses": if even a single house with a single gate already has many gates, how much more so when the family is wealthy and the houses are vast? It stands to reason that a single house with many gates would logically be immeasurable.
"Gate" refers to the path for exiting the house; since there are many paths for entering a house, the gate cannot be singular.
"Field" refers to the means of sustaining one's life; in relation to the field of life, it must not be narrow.
Furthermore, because it encompasses both the provisional and the ultimate, it is said to have "many gates.
If one relies on the four contemplations as being identical in their observation, then the gate of the chariot and the gate of the house are not different.
Regarding the phrase "from servants to fullness," the names and details of these "servants" are as explained in the seventh fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation).
Now, servants and attendants depend upon one's physical life; therefore, know that they are both auxiliary supports for the true reality of concentration and wisdom.
Because there is no deficiency in what is required, it is said that they are "complete."
Because he employs expedient means and transformations, it is said that he "harmonizes his light" and so forth.
"Xue-xue" (穴穴) means "redundant," referring also to officials outside the formal hierarchy.
Sentient beings dwell outside the rank of the sages; therefore, they are called "xue-xue."
If they do not even belong to the contemplations of other teachings, how much less could they belong to the stage of the Ultimate Sage?
"All dwellings" refers to habitation.
Because they have not emerged from the three realms but have resided within them for a long time, they are called "dwellings."
There is nothing in the world that is not thus; therefore, it is said that "all" are so.
When the Tathāgata guides sentient beings, he "unifies" and "houses" them: "unify" (tǒng) means to preside over, and "house" (jiā) also means to dwell in.
Some take the eighth consciousness as their "home," yet since all [eight] are equally subject to delusion, why speak only of the "eighth"?
The intent of the *Daochang guan* is that principle constitutes wisdom-penetration; since principle is a single gate, how could it admit of two?
Since one must exit through a gate, there are no alternative paths.
In this context, "gate" refers to the teaching;
"abode" (zhai) refers to the triple world.
"Nine hundred and six" is a textual abbreviation for "ninety-six.
Ninety-six refers to the various paths.

Just as when one wishes to leave a house there is but a single gate, though these ninety-six paths each claim to be the true path, they merely run about in a crisscrossing manner; thus, the *Sūtra of the Ninety-Six Paths* says:
"There is only one path that is correct; all others are entirely erroneous.
Some cite the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, stating:
"Each of the six teachers had fifteen disciples; together with the six teachers themselves, this makes ninety-six."
According to the *Nin-jū-roku-dō-kyō* (Sūtra of the Ninety-six Paths), there is no such statement.
That treatise represents but one perspective; how could it be that each of the six masters necessarily had exactly fifteen disciples?
Among the ninety-six [non-Buddhist] schools, there are both heterodox and orthodox views, as detailed in the third commentary on the *Zhi guan*.
The phrase "Now, to clarify" and what follows serves to refute these two schools.
This section is divided into five parts.

First, the two masters are refuted; from the words "If [it were] mere principle" onwards, the difficulties of the debate are raised first. Principle is that which is to be penetrated; if that which is penetrated (the object) is treated as the agent of penetration (the subject), then the agent of penetration would itself become the object—what, then, would there be left to be penetrated?
Since the meaning of "gate" (mēn) cannot be established, it is asked: "What is meant by 'gate'?

Following the section on "the single teaching," the next part refutes the Guangzhai [Temple] school: if that which is established as the "attainer" (the subject) does not exist, then the multitude [of practitioners] will ultimately never reach the "attained" (the goal). However, since principle does not admit of multiplicity, how could there be only a single gate?

Regarding the statement that there is "one," it is fully explained as follows in the subsequent commentary: since a house is merely a place of residence, one would expect only one to be established; yet even there it is said there are many, let alone the gates through which one passes.
This refers to the eight thousand "gates of non-duality" found in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
Now, when principle and teaching are compared, they cannot be discussed in isolation.
Next, from "Now, taking... onwards, their respective characteristics as gates are determined; that is, the teaching of the section on Principle is taken as the gate.

Since principle is one, the teaching cannot admit of two; thus, taken as a whole, it constitutes a single unity. This single phrase simultaneously refutes both schools: by adopting the "capacity" (neng) of the "appropriated" (suo), it proceeds from the capacity to the possessor of that capacity. Although this does not explicitly refute the application of wisdom at the site of enlightenment (the *bodhimaṇḍa*), when wisdom is viewed in relation to the teaching, they are equally "capacities for appropriation. Once the capacity of the teaching is abolished, the capacity of wisdom is likewise nullified.

However, wisdom must necessarily rely upon the teaching to contemplate the object; since the term "meaning" (*yi*) already encompasses both the subject and the object, one cannot say that it refers to the attainment of wisdom.

Nevertheless, this currently contradicts the scriptural text. The scripture speaks of the "gate of teaching," whereas the Master [Zhiyi] speaks of "principle and wisdom"; therefore, he likewise shares the same flaw as Guangzhai.
3. From "The text says" onwards, citations of scriptural authority are introduced.
Here, the teaching is the means of expression (*vācaka*) and *nirvāṇa* is the object expressed (*vācya*); both differ from the views of the two masters.
4. From "Furthermore, there are two gates" onwards, there is a detailed analytical explanation.

In the explanation, there are two parts. First, we distinguish between the Great and Small Vehicles: although both possess the subject and object, they are separated by a vast gulf. Therefore, it is necessary to discern the two capacities—the provisional and the real. If one recognizes these two capacities, then the two objects will be understood as they truly are. Once the real object is recognized through the provisional capacity, both the capacity and the object become the real capacity. Only after this thorough differentiation can the discussion of their ultimate convergence begin.

5. Below, the text sets forth an objection, employing the contrast between the present and the past as the basis for the challenge: the house is that which is exited from, while the carriage is that which is entered into; the house gate is the path by which one exits, whereas the carriage gate is the path by which one enters. Since these two paths are distinct and the directions of entry and exit differ, it follows that the house gate is not the carriage gate.
Therefore, the present objection states:
If the carriage, the house, and the gate are one, why has one not yet obtained the carriage even after leaving the house?
If they are [conceived as] absolute and independent, then one should now challenge [this view] by asking:

If the gate for the large carriage were not the same as the house gate, there ought to have been a separate exit when it was being pulled out; why then did he pull it out through that very same gate, and why did the elder give it back through this same gate?
He asked again:
"Having reached the gate of the house but not yet the gate of the carriage, where does one abide?
He replied:
The Great and the Small follow different paths; therefore, they are said to be distinct.
If the Small is opened up to reveal the Great, how can they be both identical and different?

Thus, I shall now explain this: if one rejects them, the carriage and the house are eternally separate; if one opens them up, the two gates are not different. Since the house and the carriage are one, how can the two gates be distinct?

Therefore, the three vehicles possess two meanings: having relied upon the teaching to leave the house, one does not see the small carts; yet, having already been matured by the two flavors in the interim, one then requests from the father the vehicle previously promised. Since it was requested, it must be granted; opening that small gate is nothing other than the Great Teaching. The minor principles beneath the gate ultimately have no separate path; since the principle is absolute and non-dual, the coarse and the subtle are of one essence. The Dharma abides in its own station, and the characteristics of the world are eternal. How could there be any distinction even within the triple world?
If there were no prior difference, what would there be to discuss regarding similarity?
Those who have perished in suffering are all gathered here today.

Regarding the phrase "the secure [state] in contrast to the insecure dharmas": the Tathāgata has already abided in the secure nirvāṇa; because his capacity meets with those impure and insecure dharmas of the five turbidities, it is called a "contrast. The same applies to the state of insecurity as well.

Regarding the statement, "The walls are an analogy for the four great elements," this should be understood as applying throughout the three realms without exception. Although the formless realm lacks the physical matter produced by the four great elements, that which is produced by the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) therein is entirely like a wall; furthermore, all three realms are sustained by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

If one considers the various schools of thought, it is more appropriate to maintain that in the formless realm the four great elements and their derived matter are not entirely absent. This interpretation is most fitting.

Regarding the phrase "desiring to cause," the subsequent contemplative understanding pertains to one's own person; whereas the former [contemplation] applies universally to both self and others across the three realms and thus belongs to the realm of phenomena (*vastu*), this contemplation of one's own body carries the meaning of contemplating the mind.
If someone were to come here and provide a complete analogy by combining both the primary and secondary retributions (*niṣyanda-vipāka*), what would be incorrect about it?
Furthermore, regarding the twenty intermediate periods of formation and destruction each, since there are no sentient beings present, how could one explain the "corruptions" (*kaṣāya*) at that time?
Because the meaning of "burning" (scorching) is somewhat remote, it is not employed here.

Therefore, the current text relies solely on the causes and effects of the primary retribution within the three realms; by subsuming the secondary environment under the primary retribution, its meaning is self-sufficient.

Regarding the phrase "suddenly" and so forth: if one considers only the beginningless continuity according to the Hīnayāna, then it would follow that [the nature] was originally present, while its moment-to-moment arising and ceasing is what is currently absent.

Now, according to the fundamental principle of the Mahāyāna, [all things] are originally non-existent; they exist due to ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore, it is said that "what was originally non-existent now exists.
Thus, the term "ignorance" encompasses both the coarse and the subtle.
Now, if one points to the coarse as being the subtle, how could there be any other way?
Yet, the phrase "originally non-existent" is a common saying among people; this is what makes it so difficult. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"That which was originally non-existent now exists, and that which was originally existent now no longer exists—regarding dharmas existing throughout the three periods of time, such a thing is impossible. Although I have here cited only a single sentence, it is related to the other three sentences; therefore, I must briefly explain it to identify its general purport.

However, this single verse appears in four places; the ancients called it the "Four Pillars of Nirvāṇa" and also the "Four Occurring Verses. Thus we know that [your] interpretation is incorrect and the chamber of Nirvāṇa is collapsing.

Regarding the "four departures," they refer to the ninth, fifteenth, twenty-fifth, and twenty-sixth [chapters]. Although their great principles are the same, there are minor differences according to the respective texts.
The ninth explains the "Bodhisattva Chapter" to clarify the meaning of differentiation and non-differentiation;
the fifteenth explains the "Brahmacarya Chapter" to clarify that attainment is itself non-attainment, and non-attainment is itself attainment.
Twenty-five, the "Lion’s Roar" Chapter, explains that existence is not fixed and non-existence is not fixed;
twenty-six, refuting the nature of fixed existence to clarify the absence of intrinsic nature.
Since ancient times, interpretations have varied according to individual perspectives. The masters of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* say:

"Prior to the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*), there is impermanence. That which is permanent is 'existent originally but absent now,' whereas that which is impermanent is 'non-existent originally but existent now.'"
It is further said:

"If afflictions existed originally but Prajñā-pāramitā is now absent, such existence and non-existence would both pertain to the past; therefore, it is impossible for any dharma to exist across the three periods of time before and after the Vajra-like Samādhi."
The Dilun masters say:
"The essence and function of the eternal dharma exist inherently but are currently absent.
Zhanran of Zhang’an challenges this, saying:
"If that which was originally hidden is now manifest, it should likewise vanish again after having been manifest.
The Tripitaka Master said:
"Sentient beings have no beginning but have an end; Nirvana has no end but has a beginning."

Now, I challenge this point: "A phenomenon that has no beginning must likewise have no end; a phenomenon that has no end must necessarily have no beginning. If afflictions had an end, they would be destructible phenomena; and if a phenomenon is destructible, it logically must have a beginning. Since having a beginning and an end both implies arising from conditions, how can you claim that Nirvana has a beginning?"

That which has a beginning must necessarily have an end, which would be identical to affliction (*kleśa*); therefore, one should say that afflictions are beginningless and their essence is precisely bodhi, and thus they have no end.
That bodhi is beginningless is precisely what afflictions are; by this principle, nirvana and samsara may also be understood accordingly.

Now, speaking in terms of the Great [Vehicle], it is for this reason that we say "originally non-existent, now existent. In reality, what is originally existent is the nirvāṇa within saṃsāra; because one follows delusion, it is currently non-existent.
Since the principle is pure and originally non-existent, yet becomes existent now due to delusion, we say "originally non-existent, now existent."
If the Lesser Master were to say:
"Because that which was originally non-existent now exists by arising from conditions,
it is called ignorance," this observation of his masters' intent would not correspond at all with the principle of Nirvana.

Zhang’an’s fivefold interpretation consists of: first, based on the three truths; second, based on the permanent and the impermanent; third, based on the three types of wisdom; fourth, based on the four *siddhāntas*; and fifth, based on the four gates.
The current text is identical in meaning to the second sense: "that which was originally non-existent now exists" implies that the permanent is itself impermanent, and so forth.

If one were to rely solely on the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) school, one should have followed the initial explanation of the verse below regarding the meaning of "long-standing," stating that the three realms are "long-standing" because they are without beginning and are not something newly created. However, as we now open the wondrous teaching (Mahāyāna), it must accord with the wondrous school; therefore, the explanation of "suddenness" states that "what was originally non-existent now exists."

However, according to the meaning of Zhan’an’s second interpretation, the text and its significance are consistent; thus, we know that for the time being, one side—impermanence—is employed, while the meaning of the other side—permanence—is temporarily set aside.

Furthermore, others have arrived here to extensively enumerate the chapters on the meaning of the eight sufferings and the four modes of birth; however, this is not the primary intent of the text, which merely seeks to inform us.

Regarding the statement, "Those without such capacity are the five hundred," the words "sons" refer generally to all while the "thirty fingers" refer specifically to a subset. Thus, we know that previously they were generally categorized among the five paths of rebirth, whereas now they are in the stage of establishing karmic conditions (*karmapratyaya*). The phrase "without such [capacity]" refers back to the preceding list; this means that for the five hundred, there is only the "direct cause" (*dharmadhātu-nimitta*), while for the thirty, there are specifically the "conditional" (*pratyaya*) and "developmental" (*paripāka*) causes.
Those listed in the text are so because these five hundred [disciples] represent the locus of the living potential for awakening.
As for the phrase "or subsumed under the Hīnayāna," this is merely due to the difference between encountering the Buddha’s era and not encountering the Buddha’s era.
Regarding the phrase "all say ten," the text collectively states that there may be ten, twenty, or even thirty;
the intended meaning is simply that each of the three vehicles has ten [stages].

Regarding the statement "all say that there is the nature of wisdom within," wisdom necessarily possesses ten types; compared to the eleven types of wisdom in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, it simply lacks the "knowledge as it truly is" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).

Regarding the "ten knowledges," these refer to conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path (*duḥkha-samudaya-nirodha-mārga-jñāna*), dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), and the knowledges of exhaustion and non-arising (*kṣaya-anutpāda-jñāna*). A brief explanation is as given in the section on the "Excellence of Knowledge" in the *Xuanwen* (The Profound Text), while a detailed exposition is clarified in the "Chapter on Knowledge" (*Jñāna-nirdeśa*) of the *Abhidharmakośa*.
That text provides a general explanation through six sections: first, the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*);

second, their mutual inclusion; third, their association with the three samādhis; fourth, their association with the faculties (*indriya*); fifth, clarifying the extent of the objects they take as conditions, and so forth. These ten knowledges (*jñāna*) are cultivated from beginning to end by the Three Piṭakas and the Three Vehicles; therefore, those of the Three Vehicles ride upon them to depart from the house of saṃsāra.
This is not the primary intent here, so there is no leisure for extensive explanation.
Regarding the phrase "bodily sensation" (*kāyavedanā*) and so forth: these are the bases upon which the inversions depend.
The section beginning with "from this" [onward] concerns the characteristics of the inversions.
This is briefly as stated in the seventh fascicle of the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* (Cessation and Contemplation) and its commentary.
Following the sequence established in the sūtras and śāstras, one must first establish the stage of the five types of mental abiding (*pañca-vinodana-citta-sthiti*).
As the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* says:

"There are two essential gateways for entering cultivation: the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*). Those in whom craving (*rāga*) or discursive thought (*vitarka*) predominates should practice accordingly.

To treat the four types of craving universally, one first contemplates a skeleton; expanding this to include the entire ocean and then contracting it again is called the stage of a beginner (*ādikarmika*)."
From the feet up to the midpoint of the head is called "already matured cultivation";
binding the mind between the eyebrows is called "transcending the stage of mental attention.
As for what is termed "desire," it refers to color, shape, honor, and exquisite touch; compared to the six [objects] in the *Mahāśāstra*, it lacks the human form, voice, and graceful gestures.
Regarding "counting the breaths" and so forth: *āna* is translated here as "sending in," and *apāna* as "sending out"; these refer simply to the inhalation and exhalation of the breath.
As for the "eight sufferings," they are the inverted fruits [of existence].
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, fascicle 12, states:
"That which is called 'suffering' has the meaning of oppression.
As for "oppression," it refers to the three types of suffering and the eight types of suffering.

Regarding the three types of suffering, they arise based on the three feelings. Suffering arising from painful feeling is called "suffering upon suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); because it arises within the desire realm and the three miserable destinies, it is termed "suffering upon suffering."
The three realms are already suffering, and the desire realm is especially so; therefore, it is called "suffering upon suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).

Pleasant sensations give rise to the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*); when pleasure perishes, the resulting suffering is equal to that of the three miserable destinies, and thus it is called "the suffering of change."
That which is suffering inherent in the neutral state is called the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), which extends throughout the formless realms (*ārūpya*).
The *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"Just as when a single eyelash is placed upon the palm of the hand, one does not perceive it, yet if that same lash is placed upon the eye, it causes injury and extreme distress."
Ordinary worldlings are like the palm of a hand; they do not perceive the eyelash-like suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Thus, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"Within the lower forms of suffering, they perversely give rise to the notion of pleasure."
Although this is discussed separately, it applies universally throughout the three realms, each possessing the three types of suffering.
As for the "eight sufferings," these are precisely birth and the others.
There are five aspects to the suffering of birth:

The suffering of a lifetime consists of five stages: first, at the time of conception; second, until the end [of life]; third, growth; fourth, emergence from the womb; and fifth, the various types [of existence].
Regarding old age, there are two kinds: moment-to-moment and throughout the entire lifespan.
Furthermore, there are two kinds: increase and destruction.
Regarding the suffering of illness, first, there is the disharmony of the four great elements, which is of two types: namely, physical illness and mental illness.
Regarding the suffering of death, there are three types:
first, karmic retribution; second, adverse conditions; and third, the passage of time.
Furthermore, there are two kinds: death due to illness and death due to external causes, and so forth.
Separation from the beloved refers to abandoning that which one cherishes; this is precisely the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
Encountering the hated and disliked refers to the suffering of mental affliction (*duḥkha-duḥkha*), for it is the mind of suffering that experiences the objects of suffering.
"Seeking and not obtaining" refers back to the separation from what is loved and the encounter with what is hated.
Regarding the "five aggregates of clinging," the sutra explains that the preceding seven [topics] constitute the five aggregates of clinging.
Kāśyapa raises an objection, saying: "This meaning is not so. As the Buddha previously taught, all sentient beings seek form; if form were suffering, they would not seek form."
The Buddha said:
"Suffering is of three kinds; these are precisely the three feelings (*vedanā*). Although one seeks them, they cannot be obtained, and thus they are not suffering as previously described.
'If one knows' refers to the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). As the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:

"Having cultivated the five cessations (pañca-samatha), one next cultivates the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna); that is, by means of calm abiding and insight (śamatha-vipaśyanā), one cultivates the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena according to their specific and general characteristics, cultivating them individually according to their specific characteristics."
